text: Every newspaper strip worth reprinting was already spoken for. So I thought, why not make our own? New stories, new characters, made for the magazine.

choices.text: What did you call your company?

text: National Allied Publications. I started it in 1934 with more ambition than money, which turned out to be a habit of mine.
Every newsstand dealer thought so. An unknown publisher with unknown characters. They looked at our books like I'd handed them a dead fish.
New Fun. February 1935. Big as a newspaper page and every strip in it brand new. Nobody had done that before, whatever anyone tells you.

choices.text: What else was different about it?

text: We sold advertising in it, which no comic book had done before. A magazine has to pay its own way somehow.
Two boys from Cleveland sent me pages. Rough, but full of energy. Siegel and Shuster. I bought their work when nobody else would.

choices.text: What did they create for you?

text: I paid them. Not always on time, I grant you. Money came in slower than it went out, and every publisher in a Depression knows that arithmetic.

choices.text: What did they create for you?

text: Their first comic pages ran in New Fun that October. Henri Duval, a swordsman, and Doctor Occult, a detective of the supernatural.
A swashbuckler in the old French style. Rough work, but you could see those boys could tell a story. I saw it before anyone else did.
A detective who fought ghosts and sorcerers. They signed it Leger and Reuths, made-up names, as young men starting out sometimes do.
New Comics followed that December, and Detective Comics in 1937. Each one cost more than the last.

choices.text: How did you pay for it all?

text: Slam Bradley, a hard-fisted private eye. The idea was mine, or so I have always said, and the Cleveland boys brought him to life. I was prouder of him than I let on.

choices.text: How did you pay for it all?
